# Overview: What biological control is and why it fits sustainable agriculture

Biological control (biocontrol) uses living organisms—predators, parasitoids, pathogens, and beneficial microbes—to suppress pest and disease populations or their impacts, reducing the need for synthetic pesticides in crop protection.<cite id="53b40a21-0">Biological control is defined as “the use of living organisms to suppress the population density or impact of a specific pest organism, making it less abundant or less damaging than it would otherwise be,” and is being embedded more strongly within IPM to reduce reliance on chemical pesticides</cite>.<cite id="726e7198-0">Because arthropod herbivorous pests account for roughly 20% of global agricultural production losses, biocontrol offers a route to resilience and sustainability by favoring local biodiversity and supporting native natural enemies through agroecosystem redesign</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Beyond pest suppression, biological control is linked to preserving biodiversity, improving soil quality, and building sustainability of farming systems</cite>.

Recent research and policy discourse reflect a broad shift from chemical-only pest management toward integrated, ecologically informed approaches in which biocontrol plays a central role.<cite id="53b40a21-0">IPM seeks to minimize synthetic pesticide use; strengthening biocontrol within IPM is a key pathway to break pest/disease/weed life cycles while adapting to local conditions and operator expertise</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Bibliometric analyses show mainstreaming of conservation biological control and landscape-scale habitat strategies into sustainable pest suppression, with ecological design and biodiversity increasingly central to the field</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Legal and environmental drivers, alongside agroecological experience, have accelerated the transition toward biocontrol and biopesticides as environmentally safe alternatives</cite>.

# Mechanisms and agent categories

Biocontrol efficacy arises from direct and indirect mechanisms acting at the plant–pathogen or plant–pest interface and within the rhizosphere. Direct mechanisms include parasitism (e.g., egg/larval parasitoids), antibiosis (production of toxins or enzyme activity), and competition for resources at infection sites.<cite id="d058798c-0">In fungi such as Paecilomyces, direct suppression can be achieved via parasitism, competition, or antibiosis</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-2">General mechanisms include competition for nutrients/space, antibiosis, parasitism, production of cell wall–degrading enzymes, and induced resistance in the plant; multiple mechanisms often act together in successful biocontrol agents</cite>. Indirect mechanisms involve plant priming and systemic resistance, where microbial signals prime defenses that constrain pathogen spread throughout the plant.<cite id="d058798c-0">Indirect suppression includes induced systemic resistance (ISR) mediated by antagonists such as Paecilomyces</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-3">Disease-suppressive soils often exhibit competition, antibiosis, and ISR-driven suppression, with the rhizosphere microbiome recruited to protect the plant</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-4">For example, Trichoderma harzianum suppresses pathogens via antibiosis, cell wall–degrading enzymes, and induction of host resistance; multiple mechanisms typically underpin effective control</cite>.

Agent categories align with strategy: classical biocontrol imports or supports specialists for target pests; augmentative biocontrol scales releases of predators/parasitoids or entomopathogenic fungi; conservation biocontrol manipulates habitat to protect and enhance native enemies and ecosystem services.<cite id="726e7198-3">Classical, augmentative, and conservation biological control are distinguished by their modes of delivery, with successful examples including host-specific parasitoids and augmentative releases of Trichogramma spp.</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-3">Biological control is a crucial component of IPM, combining natural enemies with other sustainable practices to minimize pesticides while conserving beneficial species</cite>.

# Evidence of impact: yield, pest suppression, and program benefits

Field-scale losses and environmental costs of chemical-intensive control motivate biocontrol adoption. Quantifying the problem scale underscores urgency: pests damage an estimated 20–40% of crops globally each year, with resistance, contamination, and harm to beneficials driving systemic change toward lower-external-input systems.<cite id="726e7198-3">Pests damage 20–40% of crops annually, and dependence on synthetic pesticides carries long-term costs such as resistance, soil/water contamination, and harm to pollinators and beneficial insects; biocontrol provides an environmentally compatible alternative within IPM</cite>.

Evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses shows biocontrol’s tangible contributions to crop performance. Seed treatments with beneficial microbes measurably improve establishment and yield across crops and regions, offering a scalable entry point for many smallholders. In a global meta-analysis of 396 studies, biological seed treatments increased germination by 7% (±6%), seedling emergence by 91% (±5%), plant biomass by 53% (±5%), disease control by 55% (±1%), and crop yield by 21% (±2%) relative to untreated seeds, across diverse crops, pathogens, climates, and conditions.<cite id="63942072-1">Biological seed treatments significantly improve seed germination (7±6%), seedling emergence (91±5%), plant biomass (53±5%), disease control (55±1%), and crop yield (21±2%) compared to untreated seeds across crop groups, pathogens, regions, and conditions</cite>.<cite id="63942072-2">Heterogeneity across products, pests, crops, and environments necessitates quantitative synthesis; a meta-analysis was conducted to quantify effects on germination, emergence, biomass, disease control, and yield</cite>. At the program level, documented benefits in Latin America include healthier environments, safer/nutritious food, market access, new jobs, and improved livelihoods when biocontrol is integrated into advisory services and IPM practices.<cite id="63942072-4">Implementation of biocontrol programs in Latin America yields social–economic benefits—healthier environments, safer food, market access, and improved rural livelihoods—provided farmers have access to advisory services for correct agent selection and application within IPM</cite>.

Augmentative and conservation strategies are also advancing with technology. Innovations in mass-rearing, cold storage, and delivery (e.g., drones, AI/IoT monitoring, predictive models) improve precision, scalability, and field performance while preserving environmental safety and economic viability; however, operational costs, technology access, and regulatory constraints remain barriers to broad adoption.<cite id="726e7198-2">Augmentative biocontrol is integral to sustainable pest management, yet mass production, quality consistency, storage, field performance, and costs constrain large-scale use; new technologies in rearing, genomics, and precision deployment are improving efficacy and scalability, but standardization, accessibility, and regulatory frameworks are still needed</cite>.

# Soil health and ecosystem services

Biocontrol contributes to soil and ecosystem health by enhancing biodiversity and soil quality, and by substituting chemical inputs with ecosystem processes. Conservation biological control and habitat management—cover crops, floral resources, reduced tillage compatible with enemy mobility—are central to sustaining natural enemies and soil microbiomes that regulate pests and recycle nutrients.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Biological control positively fosters agroecosystems, delivering multiple advantages—preserving biodiversity, improving soil quality, and building sustainability</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Research increasingly integrates biodiversity, habitat management, and landscape-scale strategies into sustainable pest suppression, reflecting the mainstreaming of conservation-oriented approaches</cite>.

Mechanistically, beneficial microbes and mycorrhizal symbionts improve nutrient uptake and organic matter turnover, while entomopathogenic fungi reduce the need for soil-applied fumigants that degrade soil biology. Reviews of biocontrol programs report co-benefits for soil structure and nutrient cycling alongside pest suppression, reinforcing links to long-term productivity and resilience.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Biocontrol is associated with improving soil quality and building sustainable systems</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-3">Disease-suppressive soils exhibit competition, antibiosis, and ISR, with rhizosphere microbiome dynamics central to plant health and nutrient acquisition</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-2">Plant growth–promoting bacteria provide disease control via competition, antibiosis, and signaling manipulation, illustrating microbial contributions to both defense and nutrition</cite>.

# Integration into sustainable systems: IPM and agroecology

Effective deployment hinges on integrating biocontrol within IP monitoring–decision cycles and designing landscapes that support natural enemies. IPM places biocontrol alongside cultural, mechanical, and, where needed, judiciously timed chemical control to break pest/disease/weed cycles while minimizing risks and preserving ecological functions.<cite id="53b40a21-0">IPM uses biocontrol and ecological principles to reduce chemical reliance; success depends on appropriate combinations, operator expertise, and adaptation to local conditions</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-1">Case studies in date palm systems show sustainable RPW management via integrated biological, cultural, physical, and chemical methods tailored to local environmental drivers and habitat structure</cite>.

Conservation biological control—habitat-based management—has emerged as a cost-effective lever. Increasing landscape complexity, field margins, and floral resources supports predator/parasitoid populations and pollinators, improving pest regulation with fewer inputs; this is a core tenet of ecological intensification.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Agroecosystem and habitat-based management clusters are central in the BCA/IPM literature, reflecting the rise of conservation biological control and landscape-scale strategies</cite>.<cite id="726e7198-0">Designing agroecosystems to favor native natural enemies reduces pest outbreaks and supports sustainability transitions</cite>.

Precision IPM is enhancing biocontrol timing and placement. AI, drones, IoT, and predictive models help forecast thresholds, optimize mass-rearing and release logistics, and match spatial–temporal pest windows to biocontrol agents; yet standardization and regulatory alignment are prerequisites for scaling.<cite id="726e7198-2">AI/IoT/predictive platforms and improved mass-rearing/genomic tools are improving precision deployment and field performance of biocontrol agents, but broader adoption requires standardized evaluation, regulatory clarity, and farmer support</cite>.

# Adoption barriers and enablers

Despite benefits, uptake is constrained by technical, economic, and ecological factors. Mass production, quality control, storage, environmental performance variability, and cost–effectiveness create gaps between lab promise and field practice.<cite id="726e7198-2">Barriers include mass-rearing and quality consistency, storage and field performance, and economic feasibility; advanced technologies can improve these dimensions</cite>.<cite id="726e7198-3">Augmentative releases and predator introductions require reliable production and delivery systems; current limitations hamper large-scale implementation</cite>.

Knowledge and advisory systems are critical. Farmers need guidance on agent selection, application timing, and integration into rotations and resistant varieties to achieve consistent results and avoid single-strategy stagnation that invites resistance or loss of efficacy.<cite id="63942072-0">Economic attractiveness and technical availability are essential to incentivize farmer adoption; there is need for feasible, affordable BCAs, education, and policy support</cite>.<cite id="63942072-4">Access to advisory services enabling correct agent selection and IPM application is vital to capture social–economic benefits</cite>. Market forces are shifting: regulatory tightening on pesticides, organic demand, and technology advances are expanding the biocontrol market and improving supply chains, but costs and infrastructure remain hurdles for smallholders.<cite id="726e7198-1">Market growth to 2035 (CAGR ~5.8%) is driven by the shift to organic farming, stricter pesticide regulations, IPM uptake, and advances in biocontrol technologies; AI-based monitoring and improved mass-rearing are enhancing results and supply chains</cite>.

# Risks and responsible deployment

Biocontrol is not without risks; non-target effects and introduction of invasive alien species are recognized concerns that require rigorous risk analysis and stewardship. Reviews emphasize the need to evaluate ecological interactions and evolutionary dynamics to anticipate interference, resistance, or invasions and to maintain environmental safety alongside durability of control.<cite id="726e7198-0">Despite progress, biocontrol development often underutilizes evolutionary ecology; integrating these concepts is crucial to predict interactions and sustain effectiveness</cite>.<cite id="63942072-0">Complex interactions among crops, pathogens, BCAs, and environments can lead to biological invasion or erosion of biocontrol efficacy if strategies are static; ecological evolutionary principles are needed to balance efficacy, durability, and environmental safety</cite>.

Operational risk management includes: matching agents to targets and climates; avoiding single-agent, single-site deployment; ensuring host specificity and field-release quality; and embedding biocontrol in IPM so chemical use does not suppress natural enemies. Program evaluations and regulatory frameworks (e.g., risk analysis procedures) should be multidisciplinary and long-term to capture social–economic and ecological outcomes.<cite id="63942072-4">Assessing biocontrol program impacts requires multidisciplinary teams to measure ecological, economic, and social benefits and to guide policy and finance</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-0">Conditions that hinder increased use of biocontrol include variation across regions, mass-rearing needs, and the imperative to judiciously apply chemical control technologies adapted to local conditions</cite>.

# Practical pathways for farmers and programs

- Start with diagnostics and monitoring: align biocontrol choices with pest/disease biology, local climate, and crop phenology; integrate seed treatments validated in your region to boost establishment and early vigor.<cite id="63942072-1">Biological seed treatments significantly improve germination, emergence, biomass, disease control, and yield, offering a broadly applicable first step across crops and regions</cite>.
- Enhance habitat and ecology: use flowering margins, habitat strips, and reduced-risk chemistries to sustain predators/parasitoids and suppress outbreaks; couple with resistant varieties and cultural practices for ecological intensification.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Designing agricultural environments that support natural-enemy populations underpins conservation biological control</cite>.
- Match mechanisms to problems: select parasitoids/predators for insect pests, entomopathogenic fungi for soil- and foliar-dwelling larvae, and PGPR/Trichoderma for soil-borne and foliar diseases when multi-mechanism action (competition, antibiosis, ISR) is supported by local evidence.<cite id="d058798c-2">Mechanisms such as competition, antibiosis, and induced resistance are commonly operative and often combine in successful biocontrol</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-4">Understanding mechanisms helps anticipate resistance, prevent interference, and tailor conditions for efficacy</cite>.
- Build capacity and partnerships: link growers with extension/advisory services, seed/extension supply chains, and local research to co-adapt biocontrol products and practices; document economic and environmental outcomes to catalyze investment and credit access.<cite id="63942072-4">Documenting social–economic benefits and providing advisory services can encourage policy support and finance for biocontrol adoption</cite>.

# Bottom line

Biological control is a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture when embedded in IPM and agroecology, delivering measurable gains in pest and disease suppression, crop establishment and yield, soil health, and broader ecosystem services, while reducing dependence on synthetic pesticides and associated environmental and health harms.<cite id="53b40a21-0">Strengthening biocontrol within IPM reduces pesticide dependence and advances sustainable plant protection</cite>.<cite id="63942072-1">Global meta-analysis shows biological seed treatments significantly improve crop establishment and yield</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Biocontrol is linked to biodiversity conservation and soil quality improvement, fostering sustainable farming systems</cite>. Realizing its full potential requires addressing technical, economic, and regulatory barriers through improved production and delivery systems, robust risk analysis, and farmer-centered extension and advisory support in context-specific, landscape-scale programs.<cite id="726e7198-2">Technological advances can close production and deployment gaps, but standardization, accessibility, and regulatory frameworks are needed</cite>.<cite id="63942072-0">Economic attractiveness, technical availability, education, and policy support are essential to incentivize farmer adoption and ensure environmental safety</cite>.

Title: Can biocontrol be the game-changer in integrated pest management? A review of definitions, methods and strategies
Snippet: Global agriculture is heavily dependent on sustainable plant protection. Worldwide, the concept of integrated pest management (IPM) is being followed. IPM utilizes a range of strategies, with chemical synthetic pesticides being employed only as a last resort. However, in agricultural practice, farmers continue to rely primarily on this option. To further reduce this dependence, new strategies are being sought to strengthen the use of biological control within the IPM approach including the identification of novel non-synthetic natural compounds. Here, we discuss and report on the state of the art in biological control research in areas such as biocontrol agents and application of ecological principles. These practices can help to establish sustainable plant protection systems, with the greatest impact achieved when they are used in appropriate combinations. We highlight the conditions that currently prevent or hinder the increased use of biocontrol measures. On the background of agroecological experiences, we discuss why additional advancements in plant protection practices are imperative to more effectively break the life cycles of pests, diseases and weeds. We emphasize the significance of a judicious application of chemical control technologies, adapted to local conditions. Additionally, we highlight the key role and expertise of operators in implementing these practices and their knowledge thereof.

Title: Biological control needs evolutionary perspectives of ecological interactions
Snippet: Agriculture and food systems are responsible for at least 30% of GHG emissions and are important drivers of the rapid erosion of biodiversity (Díaz et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2022). They must thus rapidly become more sustainable. Pesticides need to be severely restricted, and greater emphasis should be placed on agroecosystem redesign to reduce pest outbreaks and favor local biodiversity, including native natural enemies of pests (Tscharntke et al., 2021). Because arthropod herbivorous pests account for ca. 20% of agricultural production losses worldwide (van Lenteren et al., 2018), biological control (i.e., "The use of living organisms to suppress the population density or impact of a specific pest organism, making it less abundant or less damaging than it would otherwise be," Eilenberg et al., 2001) offers a promising solution to achieve resilience and sustainability in agricultural systems. 

Historically, biological control was strongly improved by an increasing understanding of the trophic interactions between a targeted pest and its natural enemies (DeBach & Rosen, 1974;Huffaker et al., 1976). Over the last decades, the emphasis has been placed on the influence of indirect ecological interactions on the outcome of direct interactions between pests and their enemies (Heimpel & Mills, 2017;Holt & Hochberg, 2001;Rosenheim et al., 1995). The study of these ecological processes remains an important field of research and has yielded significant progresses in classical (i.e., importing, and releasing for establishment, natural enemies to control introduced or native pests), augmentative (i.e., the supplemental release of natural enemies), and conservation (i.e., the use of methods supporting populations of natural enemies present in the agroecosystem and promoting their effectiveness) biological control programs (Heimpel & Mills, 2017). However, development of biocontrol methods has often neglected the fundamental concepts of evolutionary ecology. This is surprising as both evolutionary concepts and methods permeated agriculture for centuries for the domestication of plants and animals or to improve traits of interest.
</snippet>

Title: Artificial intelligence in the mass production of natural enemies for biological control in modern agriculture

The market is projected to grow from $19.2 billion in 2025 to $32.8 billion by 2035, indicating a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.8% over the forecast period. Key factors driving this growth are the global transition to organic farming, stringent regulations on synthetic pesticides, and an increasing awareness of integrated pest management (IPM) strategies. The pursuit of ecofriendly alternatives to chemical pesticides has led to a rising demand for raptorial insects, parasitoids, microbial products, and beneficial organisms among growers. In addition, the adoption of perfection farming and AI-based pest monitoring systems is enhancing the effectiveness of NEs-based pest control results. The growing vacuity of customized BC results, bettered massparenting ways, and distribution networks is further accelerating market expansion. Today's consumers are also willing to spend more on chemical-free or organic foods. 4 Additionally, governments and regulatory bodies worldwide are promoting biological pest control methods to reduce reliance on chemical pesticides, further supporting market expansion. For instance, the European Union (EU)'s 'Green Deal' (https://commission.europa. eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en) and China's Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.unep.org/resources/kunming-montrealglobal-biodiversity-framework)
</snippet>

Title: Recent advancements toward augmentative biological control in pest-resilient cropping systems
Snippet: Augmentative biological control (ABC) has emerged as an important component of sustainable pest management, offering an environmentally compatible alternative to conventional chemical pesticides. However, the large-scale implementation of biological control agents (BCAs) remains constrained by challenges associated with mass production, quality consistency, storage, field performance, and economic feasibility. Recent technological advances are improving the precision, scalability, and reliability of ABC systems. Innovations in mass-rearing techniques, artificial diets, and cold storage have enhanced production efficiency, while developments in genomics, microbial symbioses, RNA-based technologies, and genome editing are expanding the adaptability and efficacy of BCAs. In parallel, drone-assisted delivery systems, automated monitoring tools, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT)-based platforms, and predictive modeling are supporting precision deployment and real-time pest surveillance within integrated pest management (IPM) frameworks. This review critically evaluates these emerging technologies with emphasis on their biological efficacy, scalability, environmental safety, economic viability, and practical implementation in agricultural systems. In addition, current limitations, including high operational costs, technological accessibility, regulatory constraints, and potential ecological risks, are discussed. Integrating advanced technologies with ABC has significant potential to improve sustainable crop protection and reduce dependence on synthetic pesticides; however, broader adoption will require standardized evaluation protocols, interdisciplinary research, and stronger regulatory and farmer-support frameworks.
</snippet>

Title: Mapping Conservation Biological Control and IPM Research (2000–2025): A Bibliometric Analysis of Natural Enemies and Habitat Management
Snippet: Agriculture constitutes the cornerstone of global food provision; however, it faces daunting challenges due to pest invasions damaging 20-40% of crops every year globally, further compromising economic sustainability and food accessibility in at-risk communities [1,2]. The dependence on synthetic chemical pesticides, which is based on historical use, has generated short-term gains in protecting crop yields but this comes at a high price in the long run, including drawbacks such as increased pesticide resistance of pest species [3][4][5], contamination of soil and water resources [6][7][8], as well as negative effects to human health and non-target organisms such as pollinators and beneficial insects [9][10][11]. Such consequences have prompted a clumsy paradigm change that needs tightening to minimize ecological footprints and also support productivity [12,13]. 

Biological control is broadly categorized into three approaches: classical (introduction of exotic natural enemies), augmentative (mass release of natural enemies), and conservation (habitat manipulation to protect and enhance existing natural enemies). # Overview: What biological control is and why it fits sustainable agriculture

Biological control (biocontrol) uses living organisms—predators, parasitoids, pathogens, and beneficial microbes—to suppress pest and disease populations or their impacts, reducing the need for synthetic pesticides in crop protection.<cite id="53b40a21-0">Biological control is defined as “the use of living organisms to suppress the population density or impact of a specific pest organism, making it less abundant or less damaging than it would otherwise be,” and is being embedded more strongly within IPM to reduce reliance on chemical pesticides</cite>.<cite id="726e7198-0">Because arthropod herbivorous pests account for roughly 20% of global agricultural production losses, biocontrol offers a route to resilience and sustainability by favoring local biodiversity and supporting native natural enemies through agroecosystem redesign</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Beyond pest suppression, biological control is linked to preserving biodiversity, improving soil quality, and building sustainability of farming systems</cite>.

Recent research and policy discourse reflect a broad shift from chemical-only pest management toward integrated, ecologically informed approaches in which biocontrol plays a central role.<cite id="53b40a21-0">IPM seeks to minimize synthetic pesticide use; strengthening biocontrol within IPM is a key pathway to break pest/disease/weed life cycles while adapting to local conditions and operator expertise</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Bibliometric analyses show mainstreaming of conservation biological control and landscape-scale habitat strategies into sustainable pest suppression, with ecological design and biodiversity increasingly central to the field</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Legal and environmental drivers, alongside agroecological experience, have accelerated the transition toward biocontrol and biopesticides as environmentally safe alternatives</cite>.

# Mechanisms and agent categories

Biocontrol efficacy arises from direct and indirect mechanisms acting at the plant–pathogen or plant–pest interface and within the rhizosphere. Direct mechanisms include parasitism (e.g., egg/larval parasitoids), antibiosis (production of toxins or enzyme activity), and competition for resources at infection sites.<cite id="d058798c-0">In fungi such as Paecilomyces, direct suppression can be achieved via parasitism, competition, or antibiosis</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-2">General mechanisms include competition for nutrients/space, antibiosis, parasitism, production of cell wall–degrading enzymes, and induced resistance in the plant; multiple mechanisms often act together in successful biocontrol agents</cite>. Indirect mechanisms involve plant priming and systemic resistance, where microbial signals prime defenses that constrain pathogen spread throughout the plant.<cite id="d058798c-0">Indirect suppression includes induced systemic resistance (ISR) mediated by antagonists such as Paecilomyces</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-3">Disease-suppressive soils often exhibit competition, antibiosis, and ISR-driven suppression, with the rhizosphere microbiome recruited to protect the plant</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-4">For example, Trichoderma harzianum suppresses pathogens via antibiosis, cell wall–degrading enzymes, and induction of host resistance; multiple mechanisms typically underpin effective control</cite>.

Agent categories align with strategy: classical biocontrol imports or supports specialists for target pests; augmentative biocontrol scales releases of predators/parasitoids or entomopathogenic fungi; conservation biocontrol manipulates habitat to protect and enhance native enemies and ecosystem services.<cite id="726e7198-3">Classical, augmentative, and conservation biological control are distinguished by their modes of delivery, with successful examples including host-specific parasitoids and augmentative releases of Trichogramma spp.</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-3">Biological control is a crucial component of IPM, combining natural enemies with other sustainable practices to minimize pesticides while conserving beneficial species</cite>.

# Evidence of impact: yield, pest suppression, and program benefits

Field-scale losses and environmental costs of chemical-intensive control motivate biocontrol adoption. Quantifying the problem scale underscores urgency: pests damage an estimated 20–40% of crops globally each year, with resistance, contamination, and harm to beneficials driving systemic change toward lower-external-input systems.<cite id="726e7198-3">Pests damage 20–40% of crops annually, and dependence on synthetic pesticides carries long-term costs such as resistance, soil/water contamination, and harm to pollinators and beneficial insects; biocontrol provides an environmentally compatible alternative within IPM</cite>.

Evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses shows biocontrol’s tangible contributions to crop performance. Seed treatments with beneficial microbes measurably improve establishment and yield across crops and regions, offering a scalable entry point for many smallholders. In a global meta-analysis of 396 studies, biological seed treatments increased germination by 7% (±6%), seedling emergence by 91% (±5%), plant biomass by 53% (±5%), disease control by 55% (±1%), and crop yield by 21% (±2%) relative to untreated seeds, across diverse crops, pathogens, climates, and conditions.<cite id="63942072-1">Biological seed treatments significantly improve seed germination (7±6%), seedling emergence (91±5%), plant biomass (53±5%), disease control (55±1%), and crop yield (21±2%) compared to untreated seeds across crop groups, pathogens, regions, and conditions</cite>.<cite id="63942072-2">Heterogeneity across products, pests, crops, and environments necessitates quantitative synthesis; a meta-analysis was conducted to quantify effects on germination, emergence, biomass, disease control, and yield</cite>. At the program level, documented benefits in Latin America include healthier environments, safer/nutritious food, market access, new jobs, and improved livelihoods when biocontrol is integrated into advisory services and IPM practices.<cite id="63942072-4">Implementation of biocontrol programs in Latin America yields social–economic benefits—healthier environments, safer food, market access, and improved rural livelihoods—provided farmers have access to advisory services for correct agent selection and application within IPM</cite>.

Augmentative and conservation strategies are also advancing with technology. Innovations in mass-rearing, cold storage, and delivery (e.g., drones, AI/IoT monitoring, predictive models) improve precision, scalability, and field performance while preserving environmental safety and economic viability; however, operational costs, technology access, and regulatory constraints remain barriers to broad adoption.<cite id="726e7198-2">Augmentative biocontrol is integral to sustainable pest management, yet mass production, quality consistency, storage, field performance, and costs constrain large-scale use; new technologies in rearing, genomics, and precision deployment are improving efficacy and scalability, but standardization, accessibility, and regulatory frameworks are still needed</cite>.

# Soil health and ecosystem services

Biocontrol contributes to soil and ecosystem health by enhancing biodiversity and soil quality, and by substituting chemical inputs with ecosystem processes. Conservation biological control and habitat management—cover crops, floral resources, reduced tillage compatible with enemy mobility—are central to sustaining natural enemies and soil microbiomes that regulate pests and recycle nutrients.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Biological control positively fosters agroecosystems, delivering multiple advantages—preserving biodiversity, improving soil quality, and building sustainability</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Research increasingly integrates biodiversity, habitat management, and landscape-scale strategies into sustainable pest suppression, reflecting the mainstreaming of conservation-oriented approaches</cite>.

Mechanistically, beneficial microbes and mycorrhizal symbionts improve nutrient uptake and organic matter turnover, while entomopathogenic fungi reduce the need for soil-applied fumigants that degrade soil biology. Reviews of biocontrol programs report co-benefits for soil structure and nutrient cycling alongside pest suppression, reinforcing links to long-term productivity and resilience.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Biocontrol is associated with improving soil quality and building sustainable systems</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-3">Disease-suppressive soils exhibit competition, antibiosis, and ISR, with rhizosphere microbiome dynamics central to plant health and nutrient acquisition</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-2">Plant growth–promoting bacteria provide disease control via competition, antibiosis, and signaling manipulation, illustrating microbial contributions to both defense and nutrition</cite>.

# Integration into sustainable systems: IPM and agroecology

Effective deployment hinges on integrating biocontrol within IP monitoring–decision cycles and designing landscapes that support natural enemies. IPM places biocontrol alongside cultural, mechanical, and, where needed, judiciously timed chemical control to break pest/disease/weed cycles while minimizing risks and preserving ecological functions.<cite id="53b40a21-0">IPM uses biocontrol and ecological principles to reduce chemical reliance; success depends on appropriate combinations, operator expertise, and adaptation to local conditions</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-1">Case studies in date palm systems show sustainable RPW management via integrated biological, cultural, physical, and chemical methods tailored to local environmental drivers and habitat structure</cite>.

Conservation biological control—habitat-based management—has emerged as a cost-effective lever. Increasing landscape complexity, field margins, and floral resources supports predator/parasitoid populations and pollinators, improving pest regulation with fewer inputs; this is a core tenet of ecological intensification.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Agroecosystem and habitat-based management clusters are central in the BCA/IPM literature, reflecting the rise of conservation biological control and landscape-scale strategies</cite>.<cite id="726e7198-0">Designing agroecosystems to favor native natural enemies reduces pest outbreaks and supports sustainability transitions</cite>.

Precision IPM is enhancing biocontrol timing and placement. AI, drones, IoT, and predictive models help forecast thresholds, optimize mass-rearing and release logistics, and match spatial–temporal pest windows to biocontrol agents; yet standardization and regulatory alignment are prerequisites for scaling.<cite id="726e7198-2">AI/IoT/predictive platforms and improved mass-rearing/genomic tools are improving precision deployment and field performance of biocontrol agents, but broader adoption requires standardized evaluation, regulatory clarity, and farmer support</cite>.

# Adoption barriers and enablers

Despite benefits, uptake is constrained by technical, economic, and ecological factors. Mass production, quality control, storage, environmental performance variability, and cost–effectiveness create gaps between lab promise and field practice.<cite id="726e7198-2">Barriers include mass-rearing and quality consistency, storage and field performance, and economic feasibility; advanced technologies can improve these dimensions</cite>.<cite id="726e7198-3">Augmentative releases and predator introductions require reliable production and delivery systems; current limitations hamper large-scale implementation</cite>.

Knowledge and advisory systems are critical. Farmers need guidance on agent selection, application timing, and integration into rotations and resistant varieties to achieve consistent results and avoid single-strategy stagnation that invites resistance or loss of efficacy.<cite id="63942072-0">Economic attractiveness and technical availability are essential to incentivize farmer adoption; there is need for feasible, affordable BCAs, education, and policy support</cite>.<cite id="63942072-4">Access to advisory services enabling correct agent selection and IPM application is vital to capture social–economic benefits</cite>. Market forces are shifting: regulatory tightening on pesticides, organic demand, and technology advances are expanding the biocontrol market and improving supply chains, but costs and infrastructure remain hurdles for smallholders.<cite id="726e7198-1">Market growth to 2035 (CAGR ~5.8%) is driven by the shift to organic farming, stricter pesticide regulations, IPM uptake, and advances in biocontrol technologies; AI-based monitoring and improved mass-rearing are enhancing results and supply chains</cite>.

# Risks and responsible deployment

Biocontrol is not without risks; non-target effects and introduction of invasive alien species are recognized concerns that require rigorous risk analysis and stewardship. Reviews emphasize the need to evaluate ecological interactions and evolutionary dynamics to anticipate interference, resistance, or invasions and to maintain environmental safety alongside durability of control.<cite id="726e7198-0">Despite progress, biocontrol development often underutilizes evolutionary ecology; integrating these concepts is crucial to predict interactions and sustain effectiveness</cite>.<cite id="63942072-0">Complex interactions among crops, pathogens, BCAs, and environments can lead to biological invasion or erosion of biocontrol efficacy if strategies are static; ecological evolutionary principles are needed to balance efficacy, durability, and environmental safety</cite>.

Operational risk management includes: matching agents to targets and climates; avoiding single-agent, single-site deployment; ensuring host specificity and field-release quality; and embedding biocontrol in IPM so chemical use does not suppress natural enemies. Program evaluations and regulatory frameworks (e.g., risk analysis procedures) should be multidisciplinary and long-term to capture social–economic and ecological outcomes.<cite id="63942072-4">Assessing biocontrol program impacts requires multidisciplinary teams to measure ecological, economic, and social benefits and to guide policy and finance</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-0">Conditions that hinder increased use of biocontrol include variation across regions, mass-rearing needs, and the imperative to judiciously apply chemical control technologies adapted to local conditions</cite>.

# Practical pathways for farmers and programs

- Start with diagnostics and monitoring: align biocontrol choices with pest/disease biology, local climate, and crop phenology; integrate seed treatments validated in your region to boost establishment and early vigor.<cite id="63942072-1">Biological seed treatments significantly improve germination, emergence, biomass, disease control, and yield, offering a broadly applicable first step across crops and regions</cite>.
- Enhance habitat and ecology: use flowering margins, habitat strips, and reduced-risk chemistries to sustain predators/parasitoids and suppress outbreaks; couple with resistant varieties and cultural practices for ecological intensification.<cite id="53b40a21-4">Designing agricultural environments that support natural-enemy populations underpins conservation biological control</cite>.
- Match mechanisms to problems: select parasitoids/predators for insect pests, entomopathogenic fungi for soil- and foliar-dwelling larvae, and PGPR/Trichoderma for soil-borne and foliar diseases when multi-mechanism action (competition, antibiosis, ISR) is supported by local evidence.<cite id="d058798c-2">Mechanisms such as competition, antibiosis, and induced resistance are commonly operative and often combine in successful biocontrol</cite>.<cite id="d058798c-4">Understanding mechanisms helps anticipate resistance, prevent interference, and tailor conditions for efficacy</cite>.
- Build capacity and partnerships: link growers with extension/advisory services, seed/extension supply chains, and local research to co-adapt biocontrol products and practices; document economic and environmental outcomes to catalyze investment and credit access.<cite id="63942072-4">Documenting social–economic benefits and providing advisory services can encourage policy support and finance for biocontrol adoption</cite>.

# Bottom line

Biological control is a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture when embedded in IPM and agroecology, delivering measurable gains in pest and disease suppression, crop establishment and yield, soil health, and broader ecosystem services, while reducing dependence on synthetic pesticides and associated environmental and health harms.<cite id="53b40a21-0">Strengthening biocontrol within IPM reduces pesticide dependence and advances sustainable plant protection</cite>.<cite id="63942072-1">Global meta-analysis shows biological seed treatments significantly improve crop establishment and yield</cite>.<cite id="53b40a21-2">Biocontrol is linked to biodiversity conservation and soil quality improvement, fostering sustainable farming systems</cite>. Realizing its full potential requires addressing technical, economic, and regulatory barriers through improved production and delivery systems, robust risk analysis, and farmer-centered extension and advisory support in context-specific, landscape-scale programs.<cite id="726e7198-2">Technological advances can close production and deployment gaps, but standardization, accessibility, and regulatory frameworks are needed</cite>.<cite id="63942072-0">Economic attractiveness, technical availability, education, and policy support are essential to incentivize farmer adoption and ensure environmental safety</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Can biocontrol be the game-changer in integrated pest management? A review of definitions, methods and strategies
Snippet: Global agriculture is heavily dependent on sustainable plant protection. Worldwide, the concept of integrated pest management (IPM) is being followed. IPM utilizes a range of strategies, with chemical synthetic pesticides being employed only as a last resort. However, in agricultural practice, farmers continue to rely primarily on this option. To further reduce this dependence, new strategies are being sought to strengthen the use of biological control within the IPM approach including the identification of novel non-synthetic natural compounds. Title: Biological control needs evolutionary perspectives of ecological interactions
Snippet: Agriculture and food systems are responsible for at least 30% of GHG emissions and are important drivers of the rapid erosion of biodiversity (Díaz et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2022). They must thus rapidly become more sustainable. Pesticides need to be severely restricted, and greater emphasis should be placed on agroecosystem redesign to reduce pest outbreaks and favor local biodiversity, including native natural enemies of pests (Tscharntke et al., 2021). Because arthropod herbivorous pests account for ca. 20% of agricultural production losses worldwide (van Lenteren et al., 2018), biological control (i.e., "The use of living organisms to suppress the population density or impact of a specific pest organism, making it less abundant or less damaging than it would otherwise be," Eilenberg et al., 2001) offers a promising solution to achieve resilience and sustainability in agricultural systems. 

Historically, biological control was strongly improved by an increasing understanding of the trophic interactions between a targeted pest and its natural enemies (DeBach & Rosen, 1974;Huffaker et al., 1976). Over the last decades, the emphasis has been placed on the influence of indirect ecological interactions on the outcome of direct interactions between pests and their enemies (Heimpel & Mills, 2017;Holt & Hochberg, 2001;Rosenheim et al., 1995). The study of these ecological processes remains an important field of research and has yielded significant progresses in classical (i.e., importing, and releasing for establishment, natural enemies to control introduced or native pests), augmentative (i.e., the supplemental release of natural enemies), and conservation (i.e., the use of methods supporting populations of natural enemies present in the agroecosystem and promoting their effectiveness) biological control programs (Heimpel & Mills, 2017). However, development of biocontrol methods has often neglected the fundamental concepts of evolutionary ecology. This is surprising as both evolutionary concepts and methods permeated agriculture for centuries for the domestication of plants and animals or to improve traits of interest.

Title: Recent advancements toward augmentative biological control in pest-resilient cropping systems
Snippet: Augmentative biological control (ABC) has emerged as an important component of sustainable pest management, offering an environmentally compatible alternative to conventional chemical pesticides. However, the large-scale implementation of biological control agents (BCAs) remains constrained by challenges associated with mass production, quality consistency, storage, field performance, and economic feasibility. Recent technological advances are improving the precision, scalability, and reliability of ABC systems. Innovations in mass-rearing techniques, artificial diets, and cold storage have enhanced production efficiency, while developments in genomics, microbial symbioses, RNA-based technologies, and genome editing are expanding the adaptability and efficacy of BCAs. In parallel, drone-assisted delivery systems, automated monitoring tools, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT)-based platforms, and predictive modeling are supporting precision deployment and real-time pest surveillance within integrated pest management (IPM) frameworks. This review critically evaluates these emerging technologies with emphasis on their biological efficacy, scalability, environmental safety, economic viability, and practical implementation in agricultural systems. In addition, current limitations, including high operational costs, technological accessibility, regulatory constraints, and potential ecological risks, are discussed. Integrating advanced technologies with ABC has significant potential to improve sustainable crop protection and reduce dependence on synthetic pesticides; however, broader adoption will require standardized evaluation protocols, interdisciplinary research, and stronger regulatory and farmer-support frameworks.

Title: Mapping Conservation Biological Control and IPM Research (2000–2025): A Bibliometric Analysis of Natural Enemies and Habitat Management
Snippet: Agriculture constitutes the cornerstone of global food provision; however, it faces daunting challenges due to pest invasions damaging 20-40% of crops every year globally, further compromising economic sustainability and food accessibility in at-risk communities [1,2]. The dependence on synthetic chemical pesticides, which is based on historical use, has generated short-term gains in protecting crop yields but this comes at a high price in the long run, including drawbacks such as increased pesticide resistance of pest species [3][4][5], contamination of soil and water resources [6][7][8], as well as negative effects to human health and non-target organisms such as pollinators and beneficial insects [9][10][11]. Such consequences have prompted a clumsy paradigm change that needs tightening to minimize ecological footprints and also support productivity [12,13]. 

Biological control is broadly categorized into three approaches: classical (introduction of exotic natural enemies), augmentative (mass release of natural enemies), and conservation (habitat manipulation to protect and enhance existing natural enemies). The present bibliometric analysis focuses primarily on conservation biological control, as the retrieved literature predominantly addresses habitat management, landscape complexity, and ecosystem services [14][15][16][17]. Using biological control is also a crucial part of integrated pest management (IPM), as it employs the use of natural enemies along with other sustainable practices to minimize the use of pesticides while saving the beneficial species. Recent studies have shown that the use of ladybird beetles and lacewings as biological control agents in the control of aphids and other pests has been very successful [18,19]. Predators such as ladybirds and lacewings, along with mirid bugs, serve an important function of improving crop yield and quality by controlling aphids and whiteflies [20,21]. Tangible success stories illustrate the effectiveness of biological control across diverse systems. Title: Mapping Conservation Biological Control and IPM Research (2000–2025): A Bibliometric Analysis of Natural Enemies and Habitat Management
Snippet: A total of 1212 Web of Science-indexed publications on biological control, natural enemies, and integrated pest management (IPM) were retrieved for the period 2000-2025. The annual publication trajectory demonstrates a clear long-term expansion of the field (Figure 1c), with three discernible phases of development. In the early period (2000-2010), publication output remained low and increased gradually, indicating that research activity was still emerging and comparatively fragmented. From 2011 onward, output increased more rapidly, marking a transition into a growth phase. This acceleration is evident in the sustained rise during 2011-2016, culminating in approximately 64 publications in 2016 (Figure 1c). After 2016, annual output remained consistently elevated, with a further intensification in the most recent period. The dataset shows a pronounced increase around 2020 (approximately 91 publications), followed by continued high productivity through 2021-2024. By 2025, annual output reached approximately 110 publications, representing the highest level observed in the series (Figure 1c). The publication dynamics indicate that biological control research has shifted from a relatively limited early literature base to a mature and rapidly expanding domain in the last decade. The sustained high output after 2015, together with the recent peak, reflects the consolidation of biological control and IPM as a major research area within agricultural and ecological sciences, with increasing attention to natural-enemy-based pest regulation at both local and landscape scales (Figure 1c).

snippet.text: A total of 1212 Web of Science-indexed publications on biological control, natural enemies, and integrated pest management (IPM) were retrieved for the period 2000-2025. The annual publication trajectory demonstrates a clear long-term expansion of the field (Figure 1c), with three discernible phases of development. In the early period (2000-2010), publication output remained low and increased gradually, indicating that research activity was still emerging and comparatively fragmented. From 2011 onward, output increased more rapidly, marking a transition into a growth phase. This acceleration is evident in the sustained rise during 2011-2016, culminating in approximately 64 publications in 2016 (Figure 1c). After 2016, annual output remained consistently elevated, with a further intensification in the most recent period. The dataset shows a pronounced increase around 2020 (approximately 91 publications), followed by continued high productivity through 2021-2024. By 2025, annual output reached approximately 110 publications, representing the highest level observed in the series (Figure 1c). The publication dynamics indicate that biological control research has shifted from a relatively limited early literature base to a mature and rapidly expanding domain in the last decade. The sustained high output after 2015, together with the recent peak, reflects the consolidation of biological control and IPM as a major research area within agricultural and ecological sciences, with increasing attention to natural-enemy-based pest regulation at both local and landscape scales (Figure 1c).

documents.title: Biological control needs evolutionary perspectives of ecological interactions
documents.snippet:
Agriculture and food systems are responsible for at least 30% of GHG emissions and are important drivers of the rapid erosion of biodiversity (Díaz et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2022). They must thus rapidly become more sustainable. Pesticides need to be severely restricted, and greater emphasis should be placed on agroecosystem redesign to reduce pest outbreaks and favor local biodiversity, including native natural enemies of pests (Tscharntke et al., 2021). Because arthropod herbivorous pests account for ca. 20% of agricultural production losses worldwide (van Lenteren et al., 2018), biological control (i.e., "The use of living organisms to suppress the population density or impact of a specific pest organism, making it less abundant or less damaging than it would otherwise be," Eilenberg et al., 2001) offers a promising solution to achieve resilience and sustainability in agricultural systems. 

Historically, biological control was strongly improved by an increasing understanding of the trophic interactions between a targeted pest and its natural enemies (DeBach & Rosen, 1974;Huffaker et al., 1976). Over the last decades, the emphasis has been placed on the influence of indirect ecological interactions on the outcome of direct interactions between pests and their enemies (Heimpel & Mills, 2017;Holt & Hochberg, 2001;Rosenheim et al., 1995). The study of these ecological processes remains an important field of research and has yielded significant progresses in classical (i.e., importing, and releasing for establishment, natural enemies to control introduced or native pests), augmentative (i.e., the supplemental release of natural enemies), and conservation (i.e., the use of methods supporting populations of natural enemies present in the agroecosystem and promoting their effectiveness) biological control programs (Heimpel & Mills, 2017). However, development of biocontrol methods has often neglected the fundamental concepts of evolutionary ecology. This is surprising as both evolutionary concepts and methods permeated agriculture for centuries for the domestication of plants and animals or to improve traits of interest.

documents.title: Recent advancements toward augmentative biological control in pest-resilient cropping systems
documents.snippet: Augmentative biological control (ABC) has emerged as an important component of sustainable pest management, offering an environmentally compatible alternative to conventional chemical pesticides. Innovations in mass-rearing techniques, artificial diets, and cold storage have enhanced production efficiency, while developments in genomics, microbial symbioses, RNA-based technologies, and genome editing are expanding the adaptability and efficacy of BCAs. In parallel, drone-assisted delivery systems, automated monitoring tools, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT)-based platforms, and predictive modeling are supporting precision deployment and real-time pest surveillance within integrated pest management (IPM) frameworks. This review critically evaluates these emerging technologies with emphasis on their biological efficacy, scalability, environmental safety, economic viability, and practical implementation in agricultural systems. In addition, current limitations, including high operational costs, technological accessibility, regulatory constraints, and potential ecological risks, are discussed. Integrating advanced technologies with ABC has significant potential to improve sustainable crop protection and reduce dependence on synthetic pesticides; however, broader adoption will require standardized evaluation protocols, interdisciplinary research, and stronger regulatory and farmer-support frameworks.

Title: Biological Control of Plant Diseases: An Evolutionary and Eco-Economic Consideration
Snippet: Historically, the demand for high crop yield has been met by pesticides application, resistance gene deployment, and other approaches. However, the comprehensive benefit of these approaches has been challenged either due to their ecological impacts or long-term effectiveness [83]. Among the alternatives, biological control appears to be one of the most promising approaches for eco-friendly and sustainable agriculture to protect crop plants and safeguard food [120]. Nevertheless, currently, it is insufficient to draw a conclusion that the application of biological control could actually improve the efficiency, profit, and convenience of disease management and agricultural productivity [101]. Unexplored aspects for further research remain, including information of the mechanisms, technological traits, and farmers' applications related to natural and economic perspectives, reactions with other agricultural practices, durability, and the ecological evolution principle. 

Economic attractiveness and technical availability are essential to incite farmers to apply biological control approaches. There is much need for the provision of feasible and affordable BCAs, education, and policy support. Complex interactions among crop plants, pathogens, BCAs, and physical environments may lead to biological invasion, threatening the local ecosystem and increasing the risk of erosion or complete loss of the efficacy of biological control approaches if they are used in a single and static manner for a long term. This highlights the importance of applying the ecological evolutionary principle to synergically evaluate the efficacy, efficiency, durability, and environmental safety of biological control. Therefore, efforts should be made to build concepts to understand the ecological tolerance, social acceptability, and economic accessibility of biological control strategies.

Title: Biological seed treatments promote crop establishment and yield: a global meta-analysis
Snippet: Seeds are a vector of genetic progress and, as such, they play a significant role in the sustainability of the agri-food system. The current global seed market is worth USD 60 billion that is expected to reach USD 80 billion by 2025. Seeds are most often treated before their planting with both chemical and biological agents/products to secure good seed quality and high yield by reducing or preventing losses caused by diseases. There is increasing interest in biological seed treatments as alternatives to chemical seed treatments as the latter have several negative human health and environmental impacts. However, no study has yet quantified the effectiveness of biological seed treatments to enhance crop performance and yield. Our meta-analysis encompassing 396 studies worldwide reveals for the first time that biological seed treatments significantly improve seed germination (7±6%), seedling emergence (91±5%), plant biomass (53±5%), disease control (55±1%), and crop yield (21±2%) compared to untreated seeds across contrasted crop groups, target pathogens, climatic regions, and experimental conditions. We conclude that biological seed treatments may represent a sustainable solution to feed the increasing global populations while avoiding negative effects on human health and ensuring environmental sustainability.

Title: Biological seed treatments promote crop establishment and yield: a global meta-analysis
Snippet: Therefore, there is a need to limit or replace chemical seed treatments with other sustainable practices to achieve the same goalviz. improved seed germination, seedling emergence, biomass production, pest control, and crop yieldwith no or reduced human health and environmental impacts (Lamichhane 2020). 

Biological seed treatments contain active ingredients encompassing microbes like fungi and bacteria, as well as plant and algae extracts. Previous studies investigated the effectiveness of biological seed treatments in controlling seedand soil-borne pests including their potential to improve seed germination, seedling emergence, plant biomass development, and yield (see the list of references used in the metaanalysis). However, the type of product used for biological seed treatments, the target seed-and soil-borne pests, the climate zone, the crop group, and the experimental conditions considered in these studies are very heterogeneous. Consequently, the effectiveness of a given biological seed treatment may significantly vary across contrasted systems or conditions and, therefore, the results of individual studies are not sufficient to draw a general conclusion. Quantitative systematic review or meta-analysis is particularly useful in quantifying and synthesizing the potential of biological seed treatments on crop development and yield. Enhanced knowledge on the best performing biological seed treatments across different crop species or different environmental gradients will be instrumental in the adoption of planting biologically treated seeds. This will in turn save yields needed to feed the increasing world population while reducing environmental risk and health hazards. Several recent meta-analyses in the field of agronomy successfully quantified the impact of different cropping practices on crop development and yield (Soltani and Soltani 2015;Carrillo-Reche et al. 2018;Knapp and van der Heijden 2018;Li et al. 2020a, c). In contrast, to the best of our knowledge, no meta-analysis has been performed yet to quantify the effectiveness biological seed treatments on crop performance and yield. 

The objective of this study was to quantify, via a metaanalysis, the effectiveness of biological seed treatments in improving seed germination, seedling emergence, plant biomass development, disease control, and yield compared to untreated seeds (i.e., without application of any chemical or biological products) across contrasted environmental conditions, crop groups, and climate zones.

Title: Benefits associated with the implementation of biological control programmes in Latin America
Snippet: It is very important to ensure that farmers have adequate access to advisory services that enable them to select the correct biological control agent and apply the appropriate application technology as part of the IPM practices applied at the field level. The proper documentation of the social-economic benefits obtained from using biological control in Latin America is crucial to expand the limited information currently available. This can contribute to decision-making at a political and management level to encourage the implementation of new initiatives on sustainable production and allocate funds to favour the use of biological control. Additionally, the banks and financial entities offering credits to farmers will obtain valuable information based on the clear benefits shown, increasing credits delivered to producers for the use of green technology or to small companies for the establishment of bioproduction units for the mass production and commercialisation of biological control agents. 

Assessing the impact of biological control programmes requires a multidisciplinary approach due to the complex nature of ecological interactions and the diverse factors involved. Multidisciplinary teams, including ecologists, agricultural experts, economists, statisticians and data analysts, social scientists, and policy experts, among others, are essential to ensure and measure the benefits associated with implementation of biological control programmes. Key benefits will favour humanity in general, providing a healthier environment and contribute to safer and more nutritious food reaching markets. It also enables access to markets and new jobs, improving the living conditions of farmers and youth in rural communities. Finally, the adoption of biological control at the field level will reinforce food security and sustainable production in Latin America. the partnership and collaboration received from National Partners and Institutions, farmers' associations and all plant doctors and national coordinators of the Plantwise programme in Latin America and the Caribbean. Consequently, the effectiveness of a given biological seed treatment may significantly vary across contrasted systems or conditions and, therefore, the results of individual studies are not sufficient to draw a general conclusion. Quantitative systematic review or meta-analysis is particularly useful in quantifying and synthesizing the potential of biological seed treatments on crop development and yield. Enhanced knowledge on the best performing biological seed treatments across different crop species or different environmental gradients will be instrumental in the adoption of planting biologically treated seeds. This will in turn save yields needed to feed the increasing world population while reducing environmental risk and health hazards. Several recent meta-analyses in the field of agronomy successfully quantified the impact of different cropping practices on crop development and yield (Soltani and Soltani 2015;Carrillo-Reche et al. 2018;Knapp and van der Heijden 2018;Li et al. 2020a, c). In contrast, to the best of our knowledge, no meta-analysis has been performed yet to quantify the effectiveness biological seed treatments on crop performance and yield. 

The objective of this study was to quantify, via a metaanalysis, the effectiveness of biological seed treatments in improving seed germination, seedling emergence, plant biomass development, disease control, and yield compared to untreated seeds (i.e., without application of any chemical or biological products) across contrasted environmental conditions, crop groups, and climate zones.

documents.snippet:
It is very important to ensure that farmers have adequate access to advisory services that enable them to select the correct biological control agent and apply the appropriate application technology as part of the IPM practices applied at the field level. The proper documentation of the social-economic benefits obtained from using biological control in Latin America is crucial to expand the limited information currently available. This can contribute to decision-making at a political and management level to encourage the implementation of new initiatives on sustainable production and allocate funds to favour the use of biological control. Additionally, the banks and financial entities offering credits to farmers will obtain valuable information based on the clear benefits shown, increasing credits delivered to producers for the use of green technology or to small companies for the establishment of bioproduction units for the mass production and commercialisation of biological control agents. 

Assessing the impact of biological control programmes requires a multidisciplinary approach due to the complex nature of ecological interactions and the diverse factors involved. Multidisciplinary teams, including ecologists, agricultural experts, economists, statisticians and data analysts, social scientists, and policy experts, among others, are essential to ensure and measure the benefits associated with implementation of biological control programmes. Key benefits will favour humanity in general, providing a healthier environment and contribute to safer and more nutritious food reaching markets. It also enables access to markets and new jobs, improving the living conditions of farmers and youth in rural communities. Finally, the adoption of biological control at the field level will reinforce food security and sustainable production in Latin America. the partnership and collaboration received from National Partners and Institutions, farmers' associations and all plant doctors and national coordinators of the Plantwise programme in Latin America and the Caribbean. Title: Paecilomyces and Its Importance in the Biological Control of Agricultural Pests and Diseases
Snippet: Although many biological control mechanisms are unknown, advances in metagenomics provide some information on the plant-pathogen-antagonist interaction [66,67]. In the genus Paecilomyces, microbial mechanisms involved in pest and disease suppression have been direct, such as parasitism, competition or antibiosis, and indirect, which involve plant protection through induced systemic resistance (ISR) mechanisms [68][69][70].

Title: Paecilomyces and Its Importance in the Biological Control of Agricultural Pests and Diseases
Snippet: Although many biological control mechanisms are unknown, advances in metagenomics provide some information on the plant-pathogen-antagonist interaction [66,67]. In the genus Paecilomyces, microbial mechanisms involved in pest and disease suppression have been direct, such as parasitism, competition or antibiosis, and indirect, which involve plant protection through induced systemic resistance (ISR) mechanisms [68][69][70].

Title: Developing microbe–plant interactions for applications in plant‐growth promotion and disease control, production of useful compounds, remediation and carbon sequestration
Snippet: The efficiency of biocontrol agents for plant disease has been demonstrated and some are commercially available (Whipps, 2004;Elmer and Reglinski, 2006;Whipps and Gerhardson, 2007). General mechanisms of action for plant pathogen control include competition for nutrients and space at the infection site, antibiosis, parasitism, production of cell wall-degrading enzymes, induced resistance in the plant, and manipulation of bacterial signalling molecules. It is likely that several mechanisms of action are at work in many biocontrol agents. Compant and colleagues (2005) reviews the mechanisms of plant disease biocontrol by plant growth-promoting bacteria. Here, we discuss two mechanisms of disease control: induced resistance and manipulation of signalling molecules.

Title: Induced Systemic Resistance and the Rhizosphere Microbiome
Snippet: Microbial communities that are associated with plant roots are highly diverse and harbor tens of thousands of species. This so-called microbiome controls plant health through several mechanisms including the suppression of infectious diseases, which is especially prominent in disease suppressive soils. The mechanisms implicated in disease suppression include competition for nutrients, antibiosis, and induced systemic resistance (ISR). For many biological control agents ISR has been recognized as the mechanism that at least partly explains disease suppression. Implications of ISR on recruitment and functioning of the rhizosphere microbiome are discussed.

Title: Integrating Biological Control Agents for Enhanced Management of Apple Scab (Venturia inaequalis): Insights, Risks, Challenges, and Prospects
Snippet: BCAs and plant pathogens can engage in various interactions, employing diverse mechanisms of action. These mechanisms can be broadly categorized into direct antagonism against the pathogen, including parasitism, antibiosis, and competition; and indirect biocontrol activities, such as the induction of systemic resistance and promotion of plant growth [77,89]. In many instances, the effective control of disease by BCAs is attributed to their utilization of multiple mechanisms. For instance, T. harzianum has been demonstrated to suppress various plant pathogens by employing a combination of mechanisms including antibiosis, cell wall degrading enzymes, and the induction of host resistance [77,121]. The viability of biological control for disease reduction relies on understanding its mechanisms. This knowledge is crucial for creating conditions supporting treatment efficacy. Identifying how biocontrol agents suppress a pathogen helps anticipate resistance and prevent interference from other ecosystem components [88].

harder.brainstorming: The seed is a broad topic where a survey system can easily retrieve and summarize types of biological control agents, their mechanisms, and benefits. To increase difficulty without making it unanswerable, I could: (1) require identifying trade-offs between competing sustainability goals that biological control creates rather than just listing benefits, forcing multi-objective reasoning; (2) require explaining why biological control adoption rates remain low despite documented benefits, demanding institutional/economic analysis beyond ecological findings; (3) require synthesis of context-dependent effectiveness patterns—why certain biocontrol approaches succeed in some agroecological zones but fail in others with similar pest pressures. Option 1 is strongest because sustainability involves inherent trade-offs (productivity vs biodiversity, short-term vs long-term, economic vs ecological) that the system must synthesize and weigh rather than just catalog positive outcomes.
harder.chosen_strategy: Force recognition and analysis of inherent trade-offs between competing sustainability dimensions: require the system to identify where maximizing one sustainability objective through biological control creates tension with another sustainability goal, then explain the mechanism of conflict rather than presenting biological control as uniformly beneficial.
harder.updated_question: Where does maximizing pest suppression through biological control create trade-offs with other sustainability goals in agriculture?
harder.why_harder: Published research on biological control overwhelmingly emphasizes pest reduction benefits and frames it as a win-win sustainability solution. Trade-offs—such as specialist natural enemies reducing pest pressure but lowering overall biodiversity, augmentative releases requiring energy-intensive mass rearing that increases carbon footprint, or prioritizing pest control over pollinator conservation when agents have non-target effects—are scattered across different subfields and rarely synthesized as conflicting objectives within a sustainability framework. A survey-strong system will retrieve many papers showing biological control benefits but must recognize contradictions across studies and reason about why maximizing one dimension degrades another, rather than just aggregating positive findings.
